articles.title: What a Role Scorecard Should Contain Before You Open a Req
articles.meta_description: A role scorecard defines the outcomes, decision rights, and evidence a hire is accountable for. Here is what belongs in one, with a comparison table and an FAQ.
articles.answer: A role scorecard names the outcomes the hire owns, the decisions they can make without escalating, the evidence that will show the outcomes happened, and the constraints they inherit. A job description lists activities; a scorecard lists results. Write the scorecard before the req, because it is what makes two interviewers disagree productively.
articles.link_context: Readers working on hiring standards and talent density often want a second treatment of the same idea:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational hiring-process framework, not employment-law guidance. Job requirements, classification, pay practices, and interview questions are regulated differently by jurisdiction, and should be reviewed with a qualified employment attorney or HR advisor before use.

sections.h2: Why the scorecard has to exist before the req
paras: The failure mode in small-team hiring is not a bad candidate. It is that three people on the hiring side are quietly holding three different jobs in their heads, and none of them discover this until a finalist splits the room. A scorecard is the artifact that forces that disagreement to happen in week zero, when it is cheap, instead of in the offer meeting, when it is expensive.

It also changes what interviews are for. If the outcomes are written down, an interview stops being a conversation about impressiveness and becomes an attempt to find evidence for or against a specific claim. That is a much easier task to divide among interviewers, and a much easier one to review afterwards.

sections.h2: Where scorecards go wrong
paras: The most common mistake is writing outcomes that no one could fail. "Improve onboarding" is not an outcome; it is a direction. If you cannot describe what a clear miss would look like, the line is not doing any work and should be rewritten or deleted.

The second mistake is omitting decision rights. Two roles can share identical outcomes and be completely different jobs depending on whether the holder can change the roadmap, approve spend, or hire. Candidates read decision rights as the real seniority signal, and they are right to.

The third is treating the scorecard as a contract. It is a planning document written before anyone has met the person or the constraints they will actually face. Say so in the document, and put a review date on it.

sections.h2: Using the scorecard after the hire
paras: A scorecard that is filed away after the offer was mostly theatre. The useful pattern is to hand it to the new hire in week one and ask them to mark anything they think is wrong, missing, or impossible given what they now know. Their edits are the first real signal you get about their judgment.

Then set a review point. A re-read every 3 months is usually enough: often enough that a role that has drifted gets noticed, rare enough that nobody is renegotiating scope every week. When the reviewed scorecard no longer resembles the original, that is information about the org, not a failure of the hire.

table.caption: Job description vs role scorecard: what each document is for
rows: Outcomes and the evidence for them
The hiring panel, then the hire
Whoever owns the req, often alone
The panel together, before the req opens
Surfaces it while it is still cheap
Usually absent or implied by title
Re-read on a set cadence, edited by the hire
A clear miss can be described in one sentence

checklist.intro: Draft these in order. If a section is hard to write, that difficulty is the finding, not an excuse to skip it.
items: The mission of the role in one sentence a stranger could repeat back.
Three to five outcomes, each written so that a clear miss is describable.
For each outcome, the evidence that will show it happened and who will see that evidence.
Decision rights: what this person can decide alone, what needs a second signature, what escalates.
Constraints inherited on day one, including the budget, headcount, tooling, and commitments already made.
The two or three competencies the panel will actually interview against, and who covers each.
Explicit non-goals, so the role is not quietly widened during the process.
A review date and the name of the person responsible for reopening the document.

faq.q: How many outcomes should a scorecard have?
faq.a: Few enough that the hire can name them from memory. Three to five is a workable range for most roles. Long lists tend to be a sign that two jobs have been merged into one req, which is worth catching before the offer rather than after.

faq.q: Does a scorecard replace the job description?
faq.a: No. The job description is an external document that goes to candidates and job boards, and it usually has legal and accessibility requirements attached to it. The scorecard is an internal planning document. Keep both, and make sure the external one does not promise something the internal one contradicts.

faq.q: Who should write it?
faq.a: The panel, together, in one session. A scorecard written by one person and circulated for comment tends to collect agreement rather than disagreement, which defeats the purpose. The point of writing it jointly is to find the places where people expected different jobs.

faq.q: What if the role changes after the hire starts?
faq.a: That is normal, and it is why the document carries a review date. Record what changed and why. A role that has drifted far from its scorecard within a quarter is usually telling you something about the organization's clarity rather than about the person filling it.

articles.title: How to Design a Work Sample That Replaces a Fifth Interview
articles.meta_description: A structured work sample tests the actual job under real constraints. Here is how to scope one, what to pay for it, and how to score it without bias creeping in.
articles.answer: A useful work sample recreates one real task from the role, is scoped to a fixed time budget, is given to every finalist in identical form, and is scored against criteria written before anyone submits. If it takes more than a few hours, pay for it. If you cannot describe how you will score it, you are not ready to send it.
articles.link_context: For a related treatment of hiring standards and talent density, readers sometimes want a second perspective:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational hiring-process framework, not employment-law guidance. Unpaid work, contractor classification, intellectual property in submitted work, and accommodation obligations are regulated differently by jurisdiction and should be reviewed with a qualified employment attorney before you run a work sample.

sections.h2: What a work sample is actually testing
paras: Interviews test the ability to describe work. Work samples test the ability to do it. Those two abilities correlate less than most hiring panels assume, which is why a candidate can be articulate for four rounds and still be a surprise in month two.

The trap is building an exercise that tests something adjacent to the job: a take-home that is really a test of free time, or a live exercise that is really a test of composure while being watched. Neither is necessarily wrong, but you should know which one you are measuring, and you should not confuse it with the job itself.

sections.h2: Scoping and paying for it
paras: Scope the exercise to the shortest form that still produces a signal. Most roles can be assessed with a task in the range of one to three hours. Past that, you are selecting for candidates with unusual availability, which is a bias you did not intend to introduce.

If the exercise takes longer than a couple of hours, pay for it at a fair rate for the work, and say so up front. Paying also changes the tone of the exchange: it makes the sample feel like a trial engagement rather than an audition, and candidates tend to treat it more seriously.

Do not use a real, currently-needed deliverable. Even when the intent is honest, asking finalists to solve a live problem you would otherwise pay for reads badly, and it creates a genuine question about who owns the output. Use a sanitized version of a problem you already solved.

sections.h2: Scoring without inventing the criteria afterwards
paras: Write the scoring rubric before the first submission arrives, and have at least two people score independently before they talk. Criteria invented after you have read a submission will reliably describe the submission you liked.

Include a debrief conversation as part of the sample. Ask the candidate what they cut, what they would do with another day, and what they assumed. That conversation is often more informative than the artifact, because it exposes how they handle constraints, which is what the job will mostly consist of.

table.caption: Three work-sample formats and what each one measures
rows: How the candidate thinks under discussion
Measures composure while observed as much as skill
Selects for candidates with spare time
Hardest to schedule; needs a contract and clear IP terms
Depth of past work and honesty about their own role in it
Past work may not resemble your constraints
Written critique of an existing artifact
Standards and ability to give feedback
Rewards fluency in writing over doing

checklist.intro: Every item here has to be true before the first candidate receives anything.
items: The task is a sanitized version of real work, not a deliverable you currently need.
The time budget is stated in the brief, and the brief says what to do if they run out of time.
Every finalist receives the same brief, the same materials, and the same window.
A written rubric exists, and at least two scorers will use it independently.
Compensation is decided and communicated if the task exceeds a couple of hours.
You have said in writing who owns the submitted work and that it will not be used commercially.
An accommodation path is offered for candidates who need one.
A debrief conversation is scheduled as part of the process, not as an optional extra.

faq.q: Should work samples be paid?
faq.a: Pay for anything beyond a short exercise. Beyond the fairness argument, paying changes what you are allowed to ask for and how seriously candidates treat it. Whether payment creates a contractor relationship with tax or classification consequences depends on your jurisdiction, so confirm the arrangement with an employment attorney.

faq.q: Is a take-home better than a live exercise?
faq.a: They measure different things. Take-homes show judgment about scope when nobody is watching; live exercises show how someone reasons out loud and responds to a second opinion. If the role is mostly independent work, weight the take-home. If it is mostly collaborative, weight the live session.

faq.q: How do we keep the work sample from favouring people with free time?
faq.a: Cap the time explicitly, say in the brief that you will only assess what fits inside the cap, and score against the cap rather than against total output. Offering a scheduled window rather than an open deadline also helps candidates with fixed caregiving or work commitments.

faq.q: Can a work sample replace reference checks?
faq.a: No. A work sample shows what someone can produce in a controlled setting. References speak to how they behaved over months inside a real organization with real constraints and colleagues. The two answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other.

articles.title: How to Build a 90-Day Onboarding Plan That Produces Evidence of Fit
articles.meta_description: A 90-day plan should generate observable evidence, not just a reading list. Here is how to structure the first three months with a phase table and checkpoints.
articles.answer: Structure the first 90 days into three phases: learn the system, ship something small end to end, then own a real outcome. Each phase should end with an artifact somebody else can look at. If the plan produces only meetings and documents the new hire read, it has told you nothing about fit.
articles.anchor: A Player Mode's material on hiring standards
articles.link_context: Readers working through onboarding and performance standards sometimes want a companion treatment:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational onboarding framework, not employment-law guidance. Probationary periods, performance documentation, and termination processes are regulated differently by jurisdiction and should be reviewed with a qualified employment attorney or HR advisor.

sections.h2: What the first 90 days should produce
paras: Most onboarding plans are a list of things the new hire will be shown. That is a plan for the organization's convenience, not a plan that produces information. A better test: at the end of each phase, is there something a third person could look at and form a view about?

This matters because the alternative is a manager forming an impression from ambient signals, which is how both unfair assessments and pleasant surprises that turn out to be wrong happen. Artifacts are reviewable. Impressions are not.

sections.h2: The three phases
paras: Phase one, roughly the first three weeks, is about the system: how work arrives, who decides what, where the sharp edges are. The artifact is usually written: a summary of how something works, or a list of things that confused them. Confusion notes from a newcomer are unusually valuable and expire quickly.

Phase two, roughly weeks four to eight, is one small piece of real work carried from start to finish, including the unglamorous parts. Small end-to-end beats large partial: shipping something minor all the way through reveals more about how a person operates than contributing a slice of something big.

Phase three, roughly weeks nine to thirteen, is ownership of a real outcome with real stakes and a real deadline. This is the first phase where the scorecard outcomes should be visible. It is also the first phase where a miss means something.

sections.h2: Checkpoints and the honest conversation
paras: Put a written checkpoint at the end of each phase, and hold it even when everything is going well. A checkpoint that only happens when there is a problem becomes a signal in itself, and people learn to dread it.

The 90-day mark should include an explicit two-way conversation: what the hire has learned about the role that was not in the scorecard, and what the manager has observed. If either side is surprised at day 90, the checkpoints were not doing their job.

table.caption: A three-phase onboarding structure and the evidence each phase produces
rows: Understand how work arrives and who decides
A written summary of one system, plus a list of what confused them
Carry one small piece of work end to end
A shipped change and a short retrospective on what got in the way
Own a real outcome with a real deadline
A result measured against a scorecard outcome
Updated scorecard with the hire's own edits

checklist.h2: Set these up before day one
checklist.intro: Onboarding plans usually fail on logistics rather than on design. These are the items that most often get discovered in week two.
items: Access to every tool the role needs, requested before the start date rather than on it.
A named person other than the manager who is expected to answer small questions.
The scorecard, handed over in week one with an explicit invitation to mark it up.
A first small piece of work already identified, not chosen after they arrive.
Three checkpoint meetings on the calendar before day one.
A short list of documents worth reading, and permission to ignore the rest.
Clarity on which meetings are mandatory in the first month and which are optional.
A stated policy on how the hire should escalate when they are blocked.

faq.q: Is 90 days long enough to judge fit?
faq.a: It is long enough to see how someone works and whether they can carry something to completion. It is often not long enough to see a full outcome cycle in roles with long feedback loops, such as enterprise sales or research. Match the assessment horizon to the role's natural cycle rather than to the calendar.

faq.q: What if the new hire is blocked by us rather than by them?
faq.a: Record it at the checkpoint as an organizational finding, not a performance finding. Onboarding plans surface organizational problems at least as often as they surface individual ones, and a checkpoint that only ever produces judgments about the person is not being used honestly.

faq.q: Should the 90-day plan be shared with the new hire?
faq.a: Yes, in week one. A plan the hire cannot see is a test they cannot study for. Sharing it also lets them tell you when a phase is unrealistic given what they have found, which is information you want early rather than at day 90.

faq.q: How does this relate to a formal probation period?
faq.a: It is not the same thing. Probationary periods, if you use them, carry specific legal meaning and documentation requirements that vary by jurisdiction. Treat the 90-day plan as a management tool and confirm any formal probation structure with a qualified employment attorney or HR advisor.

articles.title: How to Tell a Performance Problem From a Role Design Problem
articles.meta_description: Before you manage someone out, check whether the role is possible. A diagnostic table separating performance issues from role design, capacity, and context failures.
articles.answer: Ask whether a strong performer with the same brief, the same authority, and the same constraints would succeed. If the honest answer is no, the problem is role design, not the person. Role design failures show up as repeated misses across different people, blocked decisions, and outcomes that depend on authority the role does not have.
articles.anchor: A Player Mode's material on hiring standards
articles.link_context: Readers thinking about performance standards and how roles are scoped sometimes want a companion view:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational management framework, not employment-law guidance. Performance management, documentation, discipline, and termination carry specific legal requirements that vary by jurisdiction, and should be handled with a qualified employment attorney or HR advisor.

sections.h2: The substitution test
paras: The single most useful question is a substitution: if you replaced this person with the strongest operator you know, holding the brief, the authority, and the constraints constant, would the outcome change? Managers often answer that question honestly and immediately, and are surprised by their own answer.

If the outcome would not change, the role is the problem. Common causes are an outcome that depends on a decision the role cannot make, a brief that quietly contains two jobs, a capacity mismatch where the work exceeds the hours available, or a dependency on another team with no shared priority.

sections.h2: Patterns that point at design rather than performance
paras: Repetition across people is the strongest signal. If the last two holders of the role struggled in similar ways, the odds that you hired badly twice in the same shape are lower than the odds that the role is shaped wrong.

Another signal is when the person's assessment of what is blocking them has been consistent and specific for weeks, and nobody has tested it. Vague complaints are weak evidence; a specific, repeated, checkable claim that has never been checked is a management gap.

A third is when success requires influence rather than authority, and nobody said so. Some roles are legitimately influence-based, but that has to be an explicit design choice, staffed by someone who was hired for it and told about it.

sections.h2: What to do with each diagnosis
paras: If it is role design, change the design before changing the person: narrow the outcomes, grant the missing decision right, or split the role. Then set a fresh review window so the change gets a fair test rather than being judged against the old expectations.

If it is genuinely performance, be direct and specific about which outcome is being missed and what a clear improvement would look like, and follow whatever documented process your organization and jurisdiction require. Ambiguity here is unkind to the person and creates legal exposure for the organization.

If it is context, such as a reorganization or a shifted priority that made the role's outcomes irrelevant, say that plainly. Letting someone believe they failed at a job that was quietly cancelled is one of the more corrosive things a manager can do.

table.caption: Diagnostic: what the same symptom means under four different causes
rows: Only this person has missed them
Previous holders missed the same ones
The record of the last two people in the role
The role has no standing to escalate
Whether the escalation path is written down anywhere
Whether a rubric or definition of done exists
Prioritization was possible and not attempted
The scorecard against a week of actual calendar time
Who believes they own the decision, asked separately
The role's outcomes no longer matter
Not a performance question at all
Not a design question either; context changed
Whether anyone told the person the priority moved

checklist.intro: Work through these in order. Each one you skip is a claim you will have to defend later.
items: Re-read the scorecard and confirm the outcome being missed is actually written in it.
Run the substitution test honestly, out loud, with one other person.
Check whether previous holders of the role struggled in the same way.
Verify the person has the decision rights the outcome requires.
Compare the brief against a real week of their calendar and workload.
Test the specific blocker they have named, rather than assessing whether it sounds convincing.
Confirm the standard was communicated before the miss, not after it.
Follow your organization's documented process, and confirm it with HR or counsel before acting.

faq.q: What if it is both a performance problem and a design problem?
faq.a: That is common. Fix the design first anyway, because a fixed design gives you a clean read on the performance question. Assessing someone against a role that was impossible produces a conclusion you cannot rely on and cannot defend.

faq.q: How long should a redesigned role get before you reassess?
faq.a: Long enough for one full cycle of the work to complete. For most operational roles that is 3 months; for roles with long feedback loops it is longer. Setting the window in advance, in writing, protects both sides from a moving target.

faq.q: Does splitting a role always solve an overload problem?
faq.a: No. Splitting adds a coordination cost and creates a new seam where work can fall through. It helps when the two halves genuinely have different outcomes and different skills. It makes things worse when the real problem was an unclear priority, because now two people are unclear instead of one.

faq.q: Who should be involved in this diagnosis?
faq.a: At minimum, one person outside the reporting line who can push back on the manager's account. Where the outcome may affect someone's employment, involve HR or a qualified employment attorney early, because process requirements differ by jurisdiction and are difficult to repair retroactively.

articles.cluster: AI in the executive operating cadence
articles.title: What an AI Coach Can and Cannot Do Compared With a Human Coach
articles.meta_description: A side-by-side comparison of AI coaching tools and human coaches across accountability, confidentiality, pattern recognition, and cost, plus when to use which.
articles.answer: An AI coach is good at availability, structure, and rehearsal: it will prepare you at midnight and never get tired of the same question. A human coach is better at noticing what you are avoiding, holding you accountable in a way that costs something, and reading context you did not report. Most people benefit from using them for different jobs.
articles.anchor: AI coach vs human coach comparison
articles.link_context: A longer side-by-side treatment of the same question exists here:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational comparison of coaching formats. Coaching is not therapy or clinical care. If you are dealing with a mental-health concern, speak with a licensed clinician rather than any coaching product, human or automated.

sections.h2: The two are not competing for the same job
paras: The framing of AI coaching as a cheaper substitute for human coaching gets the comparison wrong, because it assumes both are trying to do the same thing. In practice the value of a human coach is concentrated in a few moments per quarter, and most of what happens between those moments is structure, rehearsal, and prompting.

Structure and rehearsal are exactly what an always-available tool is good at. What it cannot do is notice the thing you did not mention, or make you feel the cost of not doing what you said you would do.

sections.h2: Where the AI version has a real advantage
paras: Availability is the obvious one, but the underlying advantage is the removal of social cost. People will rehearse an uncomfortable conversation six times with a machine and twice with a person, because the machine does not form an impression of them. For preparation tasks, that difference is worth a lot.
It is also consistent. The same framework gets applied on a bad week as on a good one, which is genuinely useful when the point of the exercise is to keep a cadence rather than to have an insight.
And it scales down to small questions. Most people will not book time with a coach to think through a two-paragraph email, but they will spend five minutes on it if the cost is zero.

sections.h2: Where the human version is not replaceable
paras: A good human coach works with what you did not say. They notice the topic you skipped, the person you never mention, the pattern across six months of conversations. A tool works with the text you gave it, and you chose that text.

Accountability is the second gap. Telling a person you will do something and then not doing it has a social cost that a chat log does not have. Whether that cost is what makes you follow through is an uncomfortable question, but it is often yes.

Confidentiality is the third, and it is practical rather than philosophical. A human coaching relationship usually comes with an explicit agreement about what is private. With a tool, the answer depends entirely on the vendor's data handling, which you should read before you put anything sensitive into it.

table.caption: AI coaching tools vs human coaches across the dimensions that usually decide it
rows: Booked sessions, commonly 45 to 60 minutes, weekly or monthly
Effectively zero, so small questions get asked
High enough that questions get batched
Only what you put in the prompt
Central to the value of the relationship
Low; no social cost to breaking a commitment
Higher; the commitment was made to a person
Applies the same framework every time
Varies with the coach's read of the moment
Depends entirely on the vendor's data policy, which you must read
Usually governed by an explicit agreement
Strong, because there is no impression to manage
Limited to what is retained and re-supplied

checklist.h2: Deciding which to use for a given task
checklist.intro: Sort the task before you sort the tool. These questions usually settle it.
items: Is the task preparation, or is it decision-making about something you have been circling for weeks?
Does the value depend on someone noticing what you left out?
Would you behave differently if a person were going to ask you about it next week?
Is the material sensitive enough that vendor data handling matters?
Do you need the same framework applied consistently, or a fresh read?
Is this a five-minute question you would never book a session for?
Does the situation involve another person's confidential information?
Are you actually looking for clinical support rather than coaching?

faq.q: Can an AI coach replace a human coach entirely?
faq.a: For rehearsal, structure, and small recurring questions, it can carry most of the load. For the parts that depend on noticing what you avoid and on accountability that costs something, it does not substitute. Most people who use both end up using them for different categories of problem rather than choosing one.

faq.q: Is coaching the same as therapy?
faq.a: No. Coaching is oriented toward goals and performance; therapy is clinical care delivered by a licensed professional and is regulated accordingly. If what you are dealing with is a mental-health concern, that belongs with a licensed clinician, not with a coaching product of either kind.

faq.q: What should I check before putting work material into an AI coaching tool?
faq.a: Read the vendor's data handling terms: whether inputs are retained, whether they are used for training, who can access them, and where they are stored. If the material includes another person's confidential information or anything covered by a contract you signed, check that contract before pasting anything.

faq.q: How do I tell whether either one is working?
faq.a: Decide in advance what would change if it were working, and pick something observable rather than a feeling. Common choices are whether a specific recurring decision gets made faster, whether a commitment you keep breaking starts holding, or whether a conversation you have been postponing actually happens.

articles.cluster: AI in the executive operating cadence
articles.title: Where to Put AI in a Weekly Operating Review Without Losing Accountability
articles.meta_description: AI belongs in the preparation and follow-up of an operating review, not in the judgment. A stage-by-stage table showing what to automate and what to keep human.
articles.answer: Put AI in the preparation and the follow-up: assembling the numbers, drafting the summary, extracting commitments, chasing what slipped. Keep it out of the judgment layer, where someone has to say what is true and own the call. The test is whether a name is attached to the decision afterwards.
articles.link_context: Readers building an AI-supported executive operating cadence sometimes want a companion resource:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational operating framework. It does not evaluate any specific AI product, and it makes no claim about the accuracy of any tool. Verify outputs before relying on them, particularly for anything with financial, legal, or personnel consequences.

sections.h2: The part of the meeting that is worth protecting
paras: A weekly operating review has one irreplaceable moment: someone looks at a number that is worse than it should be and says what they think is causing it, in front of people who can disagree. Everything else in the meeting is logistics around that moment.

The reason to be careful about automation is not that a tool would summarize badly. It is that a fluent summary can make the meeting feel complete without that moment happening. When the recap reads well, the pressure to say the uncomfortable thing drops.

sections.h2: Preparation is where the time actually goes
paras: Most of the cost of a weekly review is assembly: pulling numbers from four places, checking they agree, writing the same context paragraph again, and reminding people what they said last week. This work is repetitive, verifiable, and low-judgment, which makes it the right place to start.

Two rules make this safe. First, the assembled pack goes out before the meeting, with enough time for someone to say the numbers are wrong. Second, whoever owns each number is named next to it, so the pack has accountability attached rather than being an anonymous artifact.

Verification matters more than it feels like it should. A generated pack that is right eleven weeks running trains everyone to stop checking, which is exactly when the twelfth week matters. Keep a spot check in the process even when it feels unnecessary.

sections.h2: Follow-up is where reviews usually fail
paras: The classic failure of a weekly review is not the meeting; it is that commitments made in it evaporate by Wednesday. Extracting commitments into a tracked list, with an owner and a date, is mechanical work that almost never gets done reliably by hand.

This is a good automation target precisely because it is unglamorous and because errors are visible: if the list says something you did not commit to, you will notice. Have the extracted list confirmed by the owner rather than assumed, and let the confirmation be one click.

table.caption: Weekly operating review: what to automate, what to keep human, and why
rows: Repetitive and verifiable against the source
Owner named next to each number
A draft saves time; the framing is a judgment call
Reviewed by the owner before it goes out
Deciding what a bad number means
This is the point of the meeting
A named person states a view on the record
Deciding what to do about it
Accountability cannot be delegated to a tool
The decision is recorded with an owner
Mechanical, and errors are easy to spot
Each owner confirms their own item
Nobody does this reliably by hand
Escalation still goes to a person
Draft is fine; the send is a judgment call
A human sends it and owns the wording

checklist.h2: Guardrails to set before you automate any of it
checklist.intro: These are the things that go wrong in the second month, not the first.
items: Every number in a generated pack has a named human owner.
The pack circulates far enough ahead that someone can dispute it before the meeting.
A spot check on source data stays in the process even after several clean weeks.
Decisions are recorded with a person's name attached, never as an output of the meeting itself.
Extracted commitments are confirmed by the owner, not assumed from the transcript.
Anyone can flag a generated summary as wrong, and that flag goes somewhere visible.
Sensitive personnel or customer detail is excluded from anything sent to an external tool.
Someone reviews once a quarter whether the meeting still produces the uncomfortable moment.

faq.q: Should meeting recordings be transcribed and summarized automatically?
faq.a: It can work well for commitment extraction, but recording changes what people say. Expect more careful and less candid discussion, particularly about performance and personnel. If your review depends on candour, consider transcribing only the operational portion, and tell people clearly which parts are recorded.

faq.q: What is the first thing to automate?
faq.a: Pack assembly, because it is the largest time cost and the easiest to verify against source systems. Commitment tracking is a close second and often has a bigger effect on outcomes, since the usual failure of a weekly review is follow-through rather than analysis.

faq.q: How do we stop the summary from replacing the discussion?
faq.a: Circulate the pack as a pre-read and start the meeting at the disagreement rather than at the recap. If the first ten minutes are someone reading a summary out loud, the pack has become the meeting. A standing first question about which number people dispute helps.

faq.q: What should never go into an external tool?
faq.a: Anything covered by a confidentiality agreement, individual performance or compensation detail, unreleased financials, and customer data governed by a contract or regulation. Check your vendor terms and your own obligations before assuming a category is fine.

articles.cluster: AI in the executive operating cadence
articles.title: How to Write a Delegation Brief a Person or a Tool Can Both Execute
articles.meta_description: A delegation brief that works for an assistant also works for an AI tool. The six elements it needs, a template table, and the failure modes of each missing element.
articles.answer: A brief that either a person or a tool can execute needs six things: the outcome, the definition of done, the constraints, the inputs and where they live, the decision rights, and what to do when stuck. Most briefs contain the first and skip the rest, which is why the result comes back wrong and nobody can say why.
articles.link_context: For a related treatment of delegation inside an executive operating system:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational operating framework. It does not evaluate any specific AI product and makes no claim about tool accuracy. Verify any delegated output before relying on it, particularly where money, contracts, or personal data are involved.

sections.h2: Why the same brief works for both
paras: Delegating to a person and delegating to a tool fail for the same reason: the brief assumed context the recipient did not have. A person will usually notice the gap and ask; a tool will fill it with something plausible. That difference makes tools an unusually good test of brief quality, because the gaps come back visible.
This is worth exploiting. If you write briefs for both, the ones that come back wrong from a tool are the ones that were going to waste a colleague's afternoon anyway.

sections.h2: The element people skip
paras: The definition of done is the element most often missing. "Draft the update" has no completion condition, so the recipient invents one, and the invented one is rarely yours. Compare it with: "one page, covering the three metrics in the pack, written for the board, no recommendations." That version can be checked.

The second most skipped element is what to do when stuck. Without it, a person waits and a tool guesses. Both are expensive. A single line, naming who to ask and how long to try first, removes most of that cost.
The third is decision rights. A brief that does not say what the recipient may decide will produce either constant check-ins or unilateral choices you did not expect, depending on temperament.

sections.h2: Reviewing the result without redoing the work
paras: Review against the definition of done, in writing, before you react to the work. Reviewing against your unstated preferences is how delegation quietly turns back into doing it yourself, one round of feedback at a time.

When the result is wrong, the useful question is which element of the brief would have prevented it. That question improves the next brief. "They should have known" improves nothing and, with a tool, is not even coherent.

table.caption: The six elements of a delegation brief and what happens when each is missing
rows: What is different in the world when this is done
Activity gets delivered instead of a result
How we both know it is finished
Budget, tone, length, deadline, what not to touch
Work that is good but unusable
What to use and where to find it
Time lost hunting, or invented source material
What the recipient may decide alone
Who to ask, and after how long
Silent waiting from a person, confident guessing from a tool

checklist.h2: A brief you can write in 5 minutes
checklist.intro: Answer these six prompts in one or two sentences each. Longer is usually worse.
items: Outcome: when this is done, what is different?
Done means: the specific, checkable condition that ends the task.
Constraints: deadline, length, audience, tone, and anything off limits.
Inputs: the documents, data, or examples to use, with the actual location.
Decide alone: the choices the recipient can make without asking.
Ask first: the choices that need a second signature, and whose.
Stuck: who to contact, and how long to try first, for example 30 minutes.
Review: how you will assess the result, stated before the work starts.

faq.q: Is this not just over-specifying the work?
faq.a: Specifying the completion condition is not the same as specifying the method. A good brief is tight about outcome, constraints, and done, and deliberately silent about approach. If your brief tells the recipient how to do it step by step, you have written instructions rather than a delegation.

faq.q: How much detail does a tool need compared with a person?
faq.a: More on inputs and constraints, because it cannot walk over and ask. Less on relationship context, which it cannot use anyway. A useful habit is to write the brief for the tool first, then hand the same brief to a person and see which parts they find redundant.

faq.q: What should never be delegated to a tool?
faq.a: Anything where the cost of a confident, plausible error is high and the error is hard to detect: financial figures presented as final, legal wording, anything involving another person's private information, and communications sent under someone else's name without review.

faq.q: How do I stop the review from becoming a rewrite?
faq.a: Review against the written definition of done before you read for taste. If your objection is not covered by the definition, that is a note for the next brief rather than a correction to this one. Rewriting silently is how delegation reverts to doing the work yourself.

articles.cluster: AI in the executive operating cadence
articles.title: How to Decide Which Recurring Tasks to Automate First
articles.meta_description: Automate tasks that are frequent, stable, verifiable, and low-consequence when wrong. A scoring table for ranking candidates plus the traps in each dimension.
articles.answer: Rank candidates on four dimensions: how often the task recurs, how stable its rules are, how easily a wrong result is spotted, and what a wrong result costs. Start where frequency and verifiability are high and consequence is low. Frequency alone is the trap: a daily task with unstable rules will consume more maintenance than it saves.
articles.link_context: Readers working through operations automation for a small team sometimes want a broader library:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational operations framework. It does not evaluate or endorse any specific automation product, and it makes no claim about the reliability of any tool. Test outputs before relying on them, particularly where money, contracts, or personal data are involved.

sections.h2: Frequency is the seductive wrong answer
paras: The instinct is to automate whatever you do most. That instinct ignores maintenance. A task that recurs daily but whose rules change monthly will need attention every month, and the attention is skilled attention from whoever built it. Stability matters at least as much as frequency.

The second thing frequency hides is verifiability. If you cannot tell quickly whether the output is right, automation converts a visible cost into an invisible risk. That trade is sometimes worth making, but it should be a decision rather than a side effect.

sections.h2: The four dimensions, and what each one is really asking
paras: Frequency asks how much time is on the table. Count actual occurrences over a month rather than estimating, because estimates of one's own repetitive work are usually wrong in both directions.

Stability asks how often the rules change. A useful proxy: how many times in the last six months did someone have to explain an exception? Frequent exceptions mean the rules live in someone's head, and encoding them will freeze a version that was never correct.
Verifiability asks whether a wrong result announces itself. A generated invoice with a wrong total will get caught by the customer; a generated summary with a subtly wrong emphasis will not.

Consequence asks what a wrong result costs before it is caught. This is the dimension that should have veto power. High consequence plus low verifiability is the combination to avoid regardless of how much time is at stake.

sections.h2: Start smaller than feels worthwhile
paras: The first automation should be small enough that abandoning it costs nothing. Its real job is to teach you where your process is actually undefined, which you will discover in the first hour of trying to specify it.

Keep the manual path working in parallel for at least a few cycles. Running both is annoying and it is also the only way to find the cases the automated path handles differently without anyone noticing.
Write down who owns the automation. Unowned automations rot quietly: they keep running after the rules change, and the failure surfaces as a mysterious data problem months later.

table.caption: Scoring a task for automation across four dimensions
rows: It recurs daily or weekly, counted rather than estimated
It happens a few times a year
Sets the size of the prize
The rules have not changed in months and exceptions are rare
Someone explains an exception most weeks
A wrong result is obvious immediately
A wrong result looks exactly like a right one
Sets how much you can trust it
A mistake is embarrassing but cheap to reverse
A mistake reaches a customer, a regulator, or a bank
Holds veto power over the other three
One named person will maintain it
It is nobody's job after launch
Determines whether it survives a year

checklist.h2: Before you build the first one
checklist.intro: Work through these for the specific task you have in mind, not for automation in general.
items: Count the actual occurrences over the last 30 days rather than estimating them.
List every exception handled in the last six months, and decide which ones the automation must cover.
Describe how you will know within a day that an output was wrong.
State what a wrong output costs before it is caught, and who bears that cost.
Name the person who owns the automation after it ships.
Keep the manual path running in parallel for a defined number of cycles.
Write down the conditions under which you would turn it off.
Set a review date to check whether the rules have moved since you encoded them.

faq.q: Should we automate a task nobody understands well?
faq.a: No. Automating an undefined process encodes whatever the current practitioner happens to do, including their workarounds and their mistakes. Document the process manually first. Often that documentation alone removes most of the pain, and it will tell you whether automation is even the right answer.

faq.q: How long should the manual path run in parallel?
faq.a: Long enough to see the exceptions, which usually means several full cycles rather than several days. Monthly processes need months. Running in parallel is tedious, and it is the only reliable way to find cases where the two paths quietly disagree.

faq.q: What is the most common reason an automation gets abandoned?
faq.a: No owner. The rules change, the output drifts, nobody is responsible for noticing, and eventually someone stops trusting it and quietly reverts to doing it by hand. Naming an owner and a review date at build time prevents most of this.

faq.q: Does high consequence rule out automation entirely?
faq.a: Not necessarily, but it changes the design. High-consequence work can be automated up to a review gate, where a named person approves before anything is sent, filed, or paid. What should be avoided is high consequence combined with low verifiability and no gate.

articles.title: What Actually Drives the Cost of a Virtual Event
articles.meta_description: Virtual event cost is driven by live complexity, speaker count, rehearsal load, and post-event deliverables, not by audience size. A cost-driver table and scoping questions.
articles.answer: Audience size is one of the smaller cost drivers in a virtual event. The costs that move are live production complexity, the number of speakers who need preparation, how much is pre-recorded versus live, accessibility services, and what you expect to receive afterwards. Two events with identical attendance can differ several-fold on those variables alone.
articles.link_context: For a dedicated treatment of how virtual event production is priced:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational scoping framework. It contains no price quotations, because pricing depends on scope, region, timing, and vendor, and any figure published here would be misleading. Ask vendors for written quotes against a written scope.

sections.h2: Why headcount is the wrong first question
paras: Buyers usually open with audience size because it is the number they know. It matters for platform licensing and for moderation load, but it is close to irrelevant for the work that dominates a production budget: rehearsal, technical direction, graphics, and the hours around the live window.

A single-track session for two thousand people can be simpler to produce than a three-track programme for two hundred, because the second one has more transitions, more speakers, more things to fail, and more rooms that need someone competent watching them.

sections.h2: The drivers that actually move the number
paras: Live complexity is the largest. Every simultaneous track, every live demo, every switch between remote presenters is a transition that needs a person and a rehearsal. Pre-recording segments moves cost from the live window into editing, which is usually a good trade for risk and sometimes a good trade for money.

Speaker preparation scales with people, not with minutes. Ten speakers with five minutes each is a bigger preparation job than two speakers with an hour each, because preparation is per-person: a tech check, a rehearsal, a briefing, and a contingency plan.

Accessibility services are frequently discovered late and then paid for in a hurry. Captioning, interpretation, and accessible materials all have lead times, and treating them as an add-on rather than a line item is how they end up costing more than they should.

Post-event deliverables are the quietest driver. "We will also want the recordings edited into clips, with transcripts, by Friday" can be a substantial piece of work that was never scoped, and it is usually raised after the event.

sections.h2: How to scope so quotes are comparable
paras: Write the scope before you contact anyone, send the same document to every vendor, and allow at least 5 days for a response. Quotes built against different assumptions cannot be compared, and the cheapest one is usually the one that assumed the least.

Ask each vendor to state explicitly what is excluded. Exclusions are more informative than inclusions, and a vendor who writes a clear exclusions list is generally easier to work with than one whose proposal contains only good news.
Ask what happens if the event runs long, a speaker drops out the morning of, or a platform fails mid-session. The answers tell you whether contingency is staffed or improvised.

table.caption: Virtual event cost drivers, ranked by how much they typically move the total
rows: Multiple tracks, live demos, frequent presenter switches
Single track, pre-recorded segments played to schedule
Many speakers, each needing a check and a rehearsal
Full dress rehearsals with the whole lineup
Live captioning, interpretation, accessible materials, short notice
Booked early with the rest of the scope
Custom motion graphics, lower thirds per speaker
Standard tier that matches actual attendance
Active Q and A across several rooms
One room with a defined Q and A window
Edited clips, transcripts, analytics, fast turnaround

checklist.h2: Write these down before requesting quotes
checklist.intro: Send the same document to every vendor. Anything you leave out will be assumed differently by each of them.
items: Number of tracks and whether they run at the same time.
Number of speakers, and which of them are remote.
Which segments are live and which are pre-recorded.
Rehearsal expectations: who attends, how many, how long.
Accessibility services required, including captioning and interpretation.
Who owns chat moderation and Q and A, and during which hours.
The exact list of deliverables due after the event, and by when.
What happens if a speaker drops out on the day, and who decides.

faq.q: Does a bigger audience cost much more?
faq.a: Audience size mainly affects platform licensing tiers and moderation staffing. It has limited effect on the production work itself, which is driven by transitions, speakers, and rehearsal. It is common for a small, complex programme to cost more to produce than a large, simple one.

faq.q: Is pre-recording cheaper than going live?
faq.a: It moves cost rather than removing it: less risk and less live staffing, more editing and more scheduling. It is usually a good trade when a segment involves a demo, an unreliable connection, or a speaker who cannot attend the live window. It is a poor trade when the value of the session is the interaction.

faq.q: Why will nobody give me a price without a scope?
faq.a: Because the same phrase means very different amounts of work. A one-hour webinar with a single speaker and a three-hour multi-track programme with live demos can both be described as a virtual event. A written scope makes quotes comparable and makes the vendor accountable to something specific.

faq.q: What is the most commonly missed line item?
faq.a: Post-event deliverables, followed by accessibility services. Both are usually assumed rather than specified, and both are raised late, when there is no time to shop around. Putting them in the original scope is the cheapest thing you can do.

articles.title: What Belongs in a Run of Show Document
articles.meta_description: A run of show assigns a named person to every cue, transition, and failure path. Here is the column structure, what to rehearse, and the rows people forget.
articles.answer: A run of show is a timed, cue-by-cue script that names who does what at each moment, including what happens when something fails. At minimum each row needs a time, a duration, what the audience sees, what the audience hears, who triggers it, and the fallback. If a row has no owner, it has no plan.
articles.link_context: For the broader definition of the production work this document sits inside:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational production-planning framework. Platform features, service scope, accessibility support, and vendor responsibilities must be confirmed with the relevant provider before an event.

sections.h2: The run of show is a contract, not a schedule
paras: An agenda tells the audience what is happening. A run of show tells the production team who is responsible at each second. The difference matters most in the twenty seconds around a transition, which is where nearly every visible failure of a virtual event happens.
Because it assigns responsibility, it should be written by whoever will direct the show and reviewed by everyone named in it. A document that nobody named in it has read is decoration.

sections.h2: The rows people forget
paras: The pre-show window is the most commonly missing section: when the room opens, what is on screen, what music plays, who is watching chat, and what the holding slide says. Audiences form their impression before the content starts.

Failure paths are the second gap. Each row should have a fallback: if the video does not roll, what happens; if the presenter drops, who fills; if the demo fails, what is the alternative. Writing these takes minutes and is the difference between a recovery and a silence.

The handover to post-event is the third. Who stops the recording, who confirms it saved, who exports chat and Q and A, and who is responsible for the file existing tomorrow. Recordings are lost this way more often than anyone likes to admit.

sections.h2: Rehearsing against the document
paras: Rehearse the transitions, not the content. Speakers can be trusted to speak; the risk is in the seams. A rehearsal that runs the full programme end to end but skips the switches has rehearsed the safe part.

Run at least one rehearsal with the actual people who will press the actual buttons, on the actual platform, at roughly the right time of day. Substitutions during rehearsal reliably hide problems that appear on the day.

Give the document a version number and a single owner, and freeze it 48 hours before the show so that every later change is logged rather than absorbed. During show week it will change, and two versions in circulation is worse than an imperfect one.

table.caption: Run of show columns and what each one prevents
rows: Ambiguity across time zones and late starts
Silent overrun that eats the next segment
A held slide left up during a live speaker
Who is unmuted and what is playing
Open microphones and missing playback audio
The named person who starts the cue
Two people acting, or nobody acting
Who is on camera, backstage, or standing by
A presenter appearing before they are ready
What happens if this cue fails
Who is watching and what they are watching for
Unmoderated chat during a sensitive segment

checklist.h2: Sections to include beyond the main programme
checklist.intro: The programme itself is usually written. These are the sections that go missing.
items: Pre-show: room open time, holding screen, music, and who is watching chat.
Speaker call times and where each person waits before going live.
The exact wording of any legal, recording, or accessibility announcement.
A fallback row for every live demo, video roll, and remote presenter.
The escalation path: who to contact if the platform itself fails.
Post-show: who stops the recording and confirms the file exists.
Export owners for chat, Q and A, attendance, and analytics.
Version number, owner, and the time the current version was published.

faq.q: How detailed should the run of show be?
faq.a: Detailed enough that someone who has not attended the planning meetings could run the show from it. That is a high bar and it is the right one, because the reason you need the document is that the person who knows everything may be unavailable on the day.

faq.q: Who should own the document?
faq.a: The technical director or whoever will call the show, not the event owner. The person calling cues needs the authority to change the document during show week, and splitting that authority is how two conflicting versions end up in circulation.

faq.q: Do small webinars need one?
faq.a: A short one, yes. Even a single-speaker webinar has a pre-show window, a start cue, a Q and A transition, a close, and a recording handover. Those are the five moments that go wrong, and they take about fifteen minutes to write down.

faq.q: What is the most useful thing to rehearse?
faq.a: Transitions and failure paths. Content rehearses itself in the sense that speakers generally know their material. What nobody has practised is the ten seconds when a video does not roll, and that is precisely the moment an audience notices.

articles.title: Webinar vs Virtual Conference vs Hybrid Broadcast: How the Scope Differs
articles.meta_description: The three common virtual formats differ in production crew, rehearsal load, failure surface, and lead time. A comparison table to pick the right format for the goal.
articles.answer: A webinar is one room, one track, and a small crew. A virtual conference adds parallel tracks, a much larger speaker-preparation load, and a real programme-management job. A hybrid broadcast adds a physical room, which brings room audio, camera coverage, and the hardest problem of the three: making the remote audience feel present.
articles.link_context: For the underlying definition of the production work each format requires:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational scoping framework. It contains no pricing, and platform capabilities, accessibility support, and vendor responsibilities must be confirmed with the relevant provider before committing to a format.

sections.h2: Choose the format from the goal, not the guest list
paras: The format decision is usually made backwards: someone decides on a conference and then works out what it is for. The more useful order is to name the outcome first. If the goal is to explain one thing well to people who will not travel, a webinar is not the budget option, it is the correct option.

Formats also imply different failure surfaces. A webinar has few things that can fail and one place to watch. A conference has many rooms, and the risk is that something goes wrong in a room nobody is watching.

sections.h2: Where hybrid gets hard
paras: Hybrid is not a virtual event with a room attached. The remote audience experiences the room through a camera and a microphone, and rooms are hostile to both: audience questions are inaudible, slides are readable in the room and not on the stream, and the energy in the room does not transmit.

The recurring hybrid failure is that the remote audience becomes second class, and they know it. Fixing that requires deliberate choices: a person whose whole job is the remote audience, repeating audience questions into a microphone, and a Q and A path where remote questions are asked first rather than last.
Hybrid also doubles the rehearsal problem, because the room and the stream have to be rehearsed together, on site, with the actual audio setup.

sections.h2: Lead time is a scope decision
paras: Speaker preparation, accessibility services, and platform configuration all have lead times that do not compress well. Budget at least 3 weeks of calendar time to collect availability, run tech checks, and get materials in when the lineup is large.

When the date is fixed and close, the right response is to reduce format complexity rather than to compress preparation. A well-run single-track programme beats an under-rehearsed multi-track one, and the audience cannot see the programme you did not attempt.

table.caption: Three virtual formats compared across the variables that decide feasibility
rows: One main room, sometimes with breakouts
Programme manager, per-track producers, technical director
All of the conference roles plus on-site audio and camera
Per-track rehearsals plus a transitions rehearsal
On-site rehearsal with the room audio in place
Room audio and the remote audience feeling ignored
Captioning per track, plus accessible materials
Captioning on the stream and in the room
Longest; venue and technical survey required
An in-person moment that a remote audience must share

checklist.intro: Answer these before anyone books a venue or a platform tier.
items: What has to be true afterwards for this to have been worth doing?
Does the value come from the content, the interaction, or the room?
How many distinct audiences are you serving, and do they need different content?
How many external speakers are involved, and how much of their time can you get?
How many weeks are there between now and the date?
Who will be responsible for the remote audience specifically?
What accessibility services are required, and have they been booked?
If you had to cut the programme in half tomorrow, what would you keep?

faq.q: Is hybrid always more expensive than fully virtual?
faq.a: It carries costs that fully virtual does not: venue, on-site audio and camera, travel, and an on-site rehearsal. Whether the total is higher depends on the virtual programme it is being compared with, but hybrid rarely costs less for equivalent content, and it always adds complexity.

faq.q: When is a virtual conference the wrong choice?
faq.a: When there is one message and one audience. Parallel tracks fragment attention and multiply the preparation load, and they are worth it only when you are genuinely serving audiences with different needs. If the tracks exist to fill a day, the day is the problem.

faq.q: How do you keep remote attendees from feeling second class in a hybrid event?
faq.a: Give someone the explicit job of representing them, repeat every audience question into a microphone before answering, take remote questions first rather than last, and design slides for the stream rather than for the room. These are decisions made in planning, not fixes applied on the day.

faq.q: What is the shortest sensible lead time?
faq.a: It depends less on the format than on the number of external speakers and whether accessibility services are needed, since both have booking lead times you do not control. When time is short, reduce format complexity rather than compressing preparation, because under-rehearsed complexity is what audiences actually notice.

articles.title: How to Run Rehearsals for a Remote Speaker Lineup
articles.meta_description: Remote speaker rehearsals should be staged: tech check, content run, then transitions. A schedule table, what to test in each stage, and what to do about no-shows.
articles.answer: Split rehearsal into three stages rather than one long session: an individual tech check per speaker, a content run for timing and slides, and a transitions rehearsal with the production team. Combining them wastes everyone's time, because a tech problem in the first ten minutes destroys a session that eight people cleared their calendars for.
articles.link_context: Readers who would rather hand the production work to a partner can look at:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational production-planning framework. Platform capabilities, accessibility support, and vendor responsibilities must be confirmed with the relevant provider before an event.

sections.h2: Why one big rehearsal fails
paras: The default is to book one rehearsal and invite everybody. It reliably goes the same way: the first speaker has a microphone problem, twenty minutes disappear, and the session ends having tested nothing that mattered while eight people watched.

Staging fixes this. Tech problems get solved one-to-one, cheaply, before anyone else is in the room. By the time the group session happens, the technical baseline is known and the time can go to the thing that actually needs the group: the seams between segments.

sections.h2: What each stage tests
paras: The tech check is short and individual. Camera, microphone, lighting, connection, screen share, and the specific mechanics of the platform being used. It should end with the speaker knowing exactly which button they will press and what they will see when they do.

The content run is about timing and materials. Speakers reliably run long, and finding that out during rehearsal is much cheaper than finding out live. This is also where slide problems appear: fonts that do not travel, videos embedded in decks, and text sized for a room rather than a stream.

The transitions rehearsal is for the production team, with speakers present only for their entry and exit. This is the stage that determines whether the show looks professional, and it is the one most often skipped because it feels like it is not about the content.

sections.h2: Handling the speaker who will not rehearse
paras: Some speakers will not attend a rehearsal. Rather than treating this as a discipline problem, treat it as a risk to be designed around: put them in a slot where a technical failure is recoverable, brief their assistant, and prepare a fallback that does not depend on them.

Record a short walkthrough video that covers the same ground as the tech check so there is a self-serve option. It will not fully substitute, but it converts some no-shows into partially prepared speakers.
Where the risk is genuinely unacceptable, pre-record the segment. A pre-recorded contribution from a speaker who cannot rehearse is almost always better than a live one.

table.caption: Three rehearsal stages, who attends, and what each one is for
rows: Camera, microphone, lighting, connection, screen share, and the exact buttons they will use
Speaker plus producer, or a small group
Length of the segment plus 15 minutes
Timing, slide behaviour, embedded media, and text legibility on a stream
Production team, speakers for entry and exit only
Every switch, cue, and fallback in the run of show
Permissions, backstage flow, recording, captioning, and chat controls
Nothing changed since rehearsal on the speaker's own setup

checklist.h2: What to confirm in an individual tech check
checklist.intro: Keep it to fifteen minutes by knowing exactly what you are testing before you join.
items: Camera framing, with the speaker seated as they will actually sit.
Microphone source, and confirmation that no other device is competing for it.
Lighting, especially windows behind the speaker.
Connection stability, tested from the location they will present from.
Screen share, including a second monitor if they intend to use one.
Any embedded video or audio in their materials, played through the platform.
The exact join link, the join time, and where they wait beforehand.
Who they contact if something fails five minutes before they go live.

faq.q: How far ahead should tech checks happen?
faq.a: Far enough ahead that a discovered problem can be fixed, which usually means at least a week for anything requiring new equipment or an IT change. A tech check the day before is better than none, but it converts problems into emergencies rather than into tasks.

faq.q: Do speakers need to rehearse from the same location they will present from?
faq.a: Yes, wherever possible. Connection quality, background noise, and lighting are properties of the location rather than the person. A rehearsal from a quiet home office tells you very little about a presentation delivered from an office with a glass wall behind it.

faq.q: What if a speaker refuses to rehearse?
faq.a: Design around it rather than escalating. Place them where a failure is recoverable, brief whoever supports them, prepare a fallback, and offer a recorded walkthrough as a self-serve alternative. If the risk is unacceptable, pre-record the segment instead.

faq.q: Is the transitions rehearsal really necessary?
faq.a: It is the one that most affects how the show looks. Content is usually the part speakers have practised; the seams are the part nobody has. Skipping it saves an hour of preparation and spends it back on the day, in front of an audience.

articles.title: How to Write a Community Charter Before Choosing a Platform
articles.meta_description: A community charter states who the community is for, what members get, what the company gets, and what is out of scope. Write it before the platform decision.
articles.answer: A community charter answers four questions in writing: who this is for, what a member gets that they cannot get elsewhere, what the organization gets in return, and what the community explicitly is not. Written first, it makes the platform decision nearly mechanical. Written afterwards, it becomes a justification for a platform someone already bought.
articles.link_context: Organizations that want managed community operations rather than an internal build can look at:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational community operations framework. Community guidelines, moderation policies, data handling, and member agreements have legal implications that vary by jurisdiction and should be reviewed by qualified counsel before publication.

sections.h2: The charter exists to make later decisions cheap
paras: Community programs do not usually fail on tooling. They fail because nobody agreed what the thing was for, so every subsequent decision, from moderation to metrics to staffing, gets relitigated from scratch. A charter is the document that stops that.

It is short. One page is usually enough, with a review date set 6 months out, and longer versions tend to be aspirational rather than useful. The test of a good charter is whether it lets you say no to something plausible.

sections.h2: The four questions
paras: Who it is for should be narrow enough to exclude someone. "Our customers" is not an answer, because customers at different stages want incompatible things: newcomers want orientation, experts want peers, and putting them in one undifferentiated room usually serves neither.

What a member gets has to be something they cannot get from a search engine or a support ticket. Access to peers with the same problem, early information, or a route to the people who build the product are real answers. "Updates and announcements" is a mailing list.

What the organization gets should be stated honestly, including if the answer is retention or product feedback. Communities where the organizational motive is hidden tend to have members who work it out anyway and resent the concealment.

What it is not is the most useful section and the one most often missing. Naming what the community will not be, such as a support channel, a sales pipeline, or a place where roadmap commitments are made, prevents the most common forms of drift.

sections.h2: Then the platform question becomes easy
paras: With a charter in hand, platform selection is mostly about matching mechanics to the charter: whether members need to find each other by expertise, whether conversation should be searchable years later, whether identity should be real or pseudonymous, and where the members already are.

The most common platform mistake is optimizing for the organization's convenience, usually integration with existing tooling, over the member's likelihood of showing up. A community in a place members do not visit is a project with an owner and no participants.

table.caption: The four charter questions, a weak answer, and what a usable answer looks like
rows: Operations leads at companies past their first twenty staff
Peers facing the same problem this quarter, and direct access to the team who builds it
Earlier signal on why people churn in month three
Not a support channel, not a sales pipeline, and not where roadmap commitments are made
A named owner, with an escalation path for policy questions
A stated review date and the conditions that would trigger a change

checklist.intro: Write one or two sentences per item. Resist the urge to expand.
items: Who this community is for, stated narrowly enough to exclude someone.
What a member gets that they cannot get from search or a support ticket.
What the organization gets, stated honestly rather than diplomatically.
What this community explicitly is not.
Who owns it, and who covers when that person is away.
How moderation decisions get made and appealed.
What member data is collected, and what will and will not be done with it.
The review date, and the conditions under which the charter would change.

faq.q: Should the charter be public to members?
faq.a: Yes, in some form. Members behave better and self-select more accurately when they know what a space is for. The internal version may hold more detail about organizational goals, but if the two versions contradict each other, members will eventually notice, and that is worse than having said nothing.

faq.q: How narrow should the audience definition be?
faq.a: Narrow enough that you can name someone it is not for. A community for everyone provides nothing specific to anyone, and the early period is when specificity matters most, because a small group with a shared problem generates conversation and a large undifferentiated one usually does not.

faq.q: What if the platform decision is already made?
faq.a: Write the charter anyway. It will either confirm the choice or reveal a mismatch you can partly design around, such as adding structure that the platform does not provide. What it prevents is the more expensive mistake of building a programme whose purpose was never agreed.

faq.q: Who should write it?
faq.a: The person who will own the community, with sign-off from whoever controls the budget and from whoever will have to defend the moderation policy. Because guidelines and data handling carry legal implications, have qualified counsel review the published version before it goes out.

articles.title: What a Community Moderation Policy Needs to Cover
articles.meta_description: A moderation policy needs stated behaviours, graduated responses, an appeal route, and a record. A response ladder table and the decisions to make before launch.
articles.answer: A workable moderation policy names the behaviours that are out of bounds, sets a graduated ladder of responses, says who decides and who hears an appeal, and requires a written record of each action. Policies fail when they list values instead of behaviours, because "be respectful" cannot be applied consistently by two different moderators.
articles.link_context: Organizations that would rather buy managed community operations than staff moderation internally can look at:
articles.disclaimer: This is an educational community operations framework, not legal advice. Community guidelines, enforcement, data retention, and member removal have legal implications that vary by jurisdiction and by platform terms, and should be reviewed by qualified counsel before publication.

sections.h2: Behaviours, not values
paras: Most published community guidelines are a list of values: be kind, assume good faith, no self-promotion. They read well and they do not survive contact with a real case, because two moderators will draw the line in different places and members will experience that as arbitrary enforcement.

The fix is to write behaviours. "No self-promotion" becomes "links to your own product are fine in the introductions channel and in response to a direct question, and not in general discussion." That version can be applied by someone who joined last week.

sections.h2: A ladder rather than a switch
paras: Policies that offer only two responses, do nothing or remove the member, produce inconsistent enforcement, because most real cases do not deserve removal and moderators are reluctant to use the only tool they have.

A graduated ladder gives moderators something proportionate: a private note, a public correction, a temporary restriction, then removal. Each rung should say who can apply it, whether it is recorded, and whether the member is told.

Separate the ladder for edge cases from the ladder for clear violations. Harassment, threats, and illegal content should not be handled through the same escalating path as an off-topic post; those need an immediate route and a named decision-maker.

sections.h2: Appeals and the written record
paras: An appeal route matters more than it seems, because the main cost of a moderation error is not the error but the sense that there is nowhere to take it. The appeal should go to someone who did not make the original decision, and it should have a stated response time.

Keep a record of each action: what happened, what was done, who decided, and what the member was told. Records make patterns visible, protect moderators from accusations of bias, and are the only way a new moderator can learn what the line actually is in practice.

Decide retention deliberately. How long records are kept, who can read them, and what happens when a member leaves are data questions with legal consequences, and they should be settled before the first case rather than during it.

table.caption: A graduated moderation ladder: what each rung is for and who applies it
rows: A first, minor, probably unintentional breach
A breach others saw, where the norm needs restating
Content that cannot stay, but the member can
Yes, with the content preserved in the record
Yes, and escalated outside the moderation team

checklist.h2: Decide these before launch, not during the first case
checklist.intro: Each item here is one that becomes contentious precisely when there is no time to think about it.
items: The specific behaviours that are out of bounds, written as behaviours rather than values.
Which rung of the ladder each behaviour normally starts at.
Who is allowed to apply each rung, and who covers when they are unavailable.
How long a temporary restriction lasts by default, for example 7 days.
The route for harassment, threats, or illegal content, which bypasses the ladder.
Who hears appeals, and the stated response time.
What gets recorded for each action, and where the record lives.
How long records are kept and who can read them.
Whether moderators are identified publicly, and what support they get after a difficult case.

faq.q: Should moderation decisions be public?
